This vignette covers topics related to phylogenetic beta diversity, including calculation of pairwise dissimilarity between sites, mapping dissimilarity from focal sites, and use of these dissimilarity values in distance decay, ordination, and regionalization analyses.

To get started, let's load the `phylospatial` library, as well as `tmap` for visualization. Note that the functions covered here all require a `phylospatial` object as input; see `vignette("phylospatial-data")` for details on constructing data sets. We'll use the `moss()` example data here.

```{r setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(phylospatial); library(tmap); library(magrittr)
ps <- moss()
```

## Dissimilarity

The `phylospatial` package provides a range of methods for calculating pairwise community phylogenetic distances among locations. It can calculate phylogenetic versions of any quantitative community dissimilarity metric available trough the `vegan` package, including the various predefined indices provided through `vegan::vegdist` as well as custom indices specified through `vegan::designdist`. The default metric is Bray-Curtis distance, also known as quantitative Sorensen's dissimilarity. Additional choices allow for partitioning dissimilarity in to turnover and nestedness components. 

Dissimilarity is computed using the function `ps_add_dissim()`, which adds a distance matrix to the `dissim` slot of your `phylospatial` data set. Or if you just want the matrix itself, you can use `ps_dissim()`. 

In addition to specifying the dissimilarity index to use, these functions include options for different ways to scale the phylogenetic community matrix before calculating dissimilarity. Setting `endemism = TRUE` will scale every lineage's occurrence values to sum to 1 across all sites, giving greater weight to narrowly distributed taxa. Setting `normalize = TRUE` scales every site's total occurrence value to sum to 1 across taxa, which results in a distance matrix that emphasizes proportional differences in composition rather than alpha diversity gradients.

Let's run an example using quantitative Sorensen's index, weighted by endemism. Printing the result, we can see it now contains dissimilarity data; this is a square distance matrix with a row and column for each site:

```{r beta, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
ps <- ps_add_dissim(ps, method = "sorensen", endemism = TRUE, normalize = TRUE)
ps
```

## Focal site dissimilarity

A full dissimilarity matrix is hard to inspect directly, since it contains a value for every pair of sites. One intuitive way to explore it is to choose a focal site and map its dissimilarity to every other site, showing where on the landscape similar lineage assemblages recur. The function `ps_dissim_focal()` does this. It accepts the same `method` and scaling options as `ps_dissim()`, and gives the same values as the corresponding row of the full matrix; for the Sorensen family of indices it computes only the focal rows, so it stays fast even for large data sets. Note that it computes dissimilarity from its own arguments, rather than reusing the matrix stored by `ps_add_dissim()`.

Focal sites can be given as site indices, as a two-column matrix of coordinates in the coordinate system of the data set, or as `sf` or `SpatVector` points, which are reprojected as needed. Let's compare two focal sites, one in the Sierra Nevada and one in the Klamath Mountains, specified by longitude and latitude:

```{r focal, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
focal <- sf::st_as_sf(data.frame(site = c("Sierra Nevada", "Klamath Mountains"),
                                 lon = c(-119.6, -123.5), lat = c(37.8, 41.5)),
                      coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)

fd <- ps_dissim_focal(ps, focal, method = "sorensen")
names(fd) <- focal$site

tm_shape(fd) +
      tm_raster(col.scale = tm_scale_continuous(values = "brewer.yl_gn_bu", limits = c(0, 1)),
                col.legend = tm_legend(title = "dissimilarity"),
                col.free = FALSE) +
      tm_shape(focal) +
      tm_dots(fill = "red", size = 0.5) +
      tm_title("Phylogenetic dissimilarity from focal sites")
```

Dissimilarity is zero at each focal site and generally rises with distance, but not uniformly: the Sierra Nevada site is more similar to the distant northern mountains than to the nearby Central Valley, and both sites are most dissimilar from the southern deserts. Patterns like these show which parts of the landscape share a site's evolutionary history, and how sharply composition changes along environmental gradients.

As with `ps_dissim()`, Sorensen's dissimilarity can be partitioned into turnover and nestedness components. The turnover component reflects replacement of lineages by different lineages, while the nestedness component reflects sites holding subsets of one another's lineages. Mapping both for the Sierra Nevada site shows that most of its dissimilarity from other sites is due to nestedness: this site is rich in lineages, and other sites mostly hold subsets of them.

`ps_dissim_focal()` also offers one index that isn't available in `ps_dissim()`: `method = "focal_difference"`, the fraction of the focal site's branch length that is absent from each other site. Unlike symmetric indices, it ignores lineages found only at the other site, so a species-rich site that contains all of the focal site's lineages has a value of zero. Because it has a direction, it is only defined relative to a focal site. It is the complement of a phylogenetic, quantitative version of a dispersion field (Graves & Rahbek 2005, *PNAS* 102:7871-7876), the overlapping ranges of all lineages present at the focal site.

```{r focal_methods, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
methods <- c("sorensen", "sorensen_turnover", "sorensen_nestedness", "focal_difference")
fm <- lapply(methods, function(m) ps_dissim_focal(ps, focal[1, ], method = m)) %>%
      terra::rast()
names(fm) <- methods

tm_shape(fm) +
      tm_raster(col.scale = tm_scale_continuous(values = "brewer.yl_gn_bu", limits = c(0, 1)),
                col.legend = tm_legend(title = "dissimilarity"),
                col.free = FALSE) +
      tm_shape(focal[1, ]) +
      tm_dots(fill = "red", size = 0.5) +
      tm_title("Dissimilarity from the Sierra Nevada site")
```

The difference between symmetric and focal indices is clearest for a species-poor focal site. Let's compare Sorensen's dissimilarity and `focal_difference` for a site in the Mojave Desert:

```{r focal_desert, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
desert <- sf::st_as_sf(data.frame(lon = -116, lat = 34.6),
                       coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)
dd <- c(ps_dissim_focal(ps, desert, method = "sorensen"),
        ps_dissim_focal(ps, desert, method = "focal_difference"))
names(dd) <- c("sorensen", "focal_difference")

tm_shape(dd) +
      tm_raster(col.scale = tm_scale_continuous(values = "brewer.yl_gn_bu", limits = c(0, 1)),
                col.legend = tm_legend(title = "dissimilarity"),
                col.free = FALSE) +
      tm_shape(desert) +
      tm_dots(fill = "red", size = 0.5) +
      tm_title("Dissimilarity from a desert site")
```

Sorensen's index rates the lineage-rich northern mountains as highly dissimilar from the desert site, because they hold many lineages the desert site lacks. But `focal_difference` shows that the desert site's own lineages occur nearly everywhere: its assemblage is largely a subset of the state's moss flora, and its lineages are missing mainly from parts of the Central Valley and the far southeastern deserts.

## Distance decay

One frequent use of dissimilarity matrices is to analyze how commmunity phylogentic similarity declines with geographic distance, environmental difference, or other geographic properties. Common methods for this kind of analysis include generalized dissimilarity modeling and partial Mantel tests. 

Here let's just visualize how phylogenetic turnover changes with the distance between sites. We can compute a pairwise geographic distance matrix using `ps_geodist()`. Let's also compare this to non-phylogenetic species turnover, which we can compute by specifying `tips_only = TRUE`. We can summarize the pattern with a LOESS curve: 

```{r geodist, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
phy_beta <- as.vector(ps_dissim(ps, method = "sorensen"))
spp_beta <- as.vector(ps_dissim(ps, method = "sorensen", tips_only = TRUE))
geo_dist <- as.vector(ps_geodist(ps)) / 1000  # convert to km

# subsample for plotting (full pairwise set is huge)
ss <- sample(length(phy_beta), 5000)

plot(geo_dist[ss], phy_beta[ss],
     pch = ".", col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.3),
     xlab = "Geographic distance (km)",
     ylab = "Dissimilarity",
     ylim = c(0, 1))
points(geo_dist[ss], spp_beta[ss],
       pch = ".", col = adjustcolor("tomato", 0.3))
 
# loess trend lines
lo_phy <- loess(phy_beta[ss] ~ geo_dist[ss])
lo_spp <- loess(spp_beta[ss] ~ geo_dist[ss])
ox <- order(geo_dist[ss])
lines(geo_dist[ss][ox], predict(lo_phy)[ox], col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
lines(geo_dist[ss][ox], predict(lo_spp)[ox], col = "tomato", lwd = 2)
 
legend("bottomright",
       legend = c("Phylogenetic", "Species"),
       col = c("steelblue", "tomato"),
       lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

## Ordination

Additional approaches for assessing spatial turnover patterns include ordination or clustering, both of which reduce a dissimilarity matrix into a lower-dimensional summary. Ordination, which is implemented in the function `ps_ordinate()`, identifies the dominant axes of variation in phylogenetic turnover, which can then be used for visualization or analysis. The funtion offers various ordination methods. Let's perform a PCA, and make maps of the first four dimensions:

```{r ordinate, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
ps %>%
      ps_ordinate(method = "pca", k = 4) %>%
      tm_shape() +
      tm_raster(col.scale = tm_scale_continuous(values = "brewer.pi_yg"),
                col.free = FALSE) +
      tm_title("Phylogenetic community ordination")
```

We can also qualitatively visualize compositional patterns by converting ordination axes to a set of colors representing how similar two sites are to each other, using the `ps_rgb()` function. Let's do that here, using the `"cmds"` (classical multidimensional scaling) ordination algorithm, and then plot the result using `tmap::tm_rgb()`:

```{r rgb, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
ps %>%
      ps_rgb(method = "cmds") %>%
      tm_shape() +
      tm_rgb(col.scale = tm_scale_rgb(max_color_value = 1), 
             interpolate = FALSE) +
      tm_title("Phylogenetic community ordination")
```



## Regionalization

We can also perform a more formal cluster analysis that splits the landscape into a set of evolutionary bioregions, using the `ps_regions()` function. To do this, we need to specify the clustering `method` and the number of clusters (`k`). Choices of method include k-means and various hierarchical clustering methods; note that results are sometimes highly sensitive to which method is selected. The hierarchical methods require a dissimilarity matrix calculated by first running `ps_add_dissim()`, while k-means does not.

Choosing `k` is usually subjective. Many alternative methods have been proposed in the literature to identify the "optimal" number of clusters in a data set, but ecological data are often inherently characterized by continuous gradients rather than discrete provinces, in which case no value of `k` may clearly fit best. You can use the function `ps_regions_eval()` to help evaluate how well different choices for `k` fit the data by comparing the variance explained by different numbers of clusters. Let's do that here, using the `"average"` hierarchical clustering method:

```{r k, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
ps_regions_eval(ps, k = 1:15, plot = TRUE, method = "average")
```
From the evaluation plot, it looks like a value of `k = 4` stands out as the most distinct "elbow" in explained variance ("SSE"), with near-maximum distance to the 1:1 line ("dist11"), and with more negative "curvature" than its neighbors, though other choices could also be reasonable. Let's generate results for four regions, and then make a map of these zones:

```{r regions, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
ps %>%
      ps_regions(k = 4, method = "average") %>%
      tm_shape() +
      tm_raster(col.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = "brewer.dark2"),
                col.legend = tm_legend(show = FALSE)) +
      tm_title("phylogenetic region")
```
